lessons.title: Emotions
lessons.scenario: Smarty meets the cast backstage at the theatre before their first rehearsal.

items.example: Ben is angry because he lost his notebook.
items.note: Say 'angry' when someone is mad because something bad happened.

image.describe: a brown cat with furrowed eyebrows and crossed arms frowning next to a dropped notebook

items.example: Sam feels jealous of Leo because Leo has the big part.
items.note: Use 'jealous' when you want something that another person has.

image.describe: a grey cat peeking from behind a stage curtain looking envious at a friend holding a shiny crown

items.example: Leo is proud of his new costume.
items.note: Say 'proud' when you feel great about something good you or a friend did.

image.describe: an orange cat standing tall on a wooden stage smiling brightly in a royal cape

items.example: Mia is nervous before she goes on stage.
items.note: Use 'nervous' when you feel a bit scared or worried before something big.

image.describe: a white cat peeking nervously from behind a velvet theatre curtain at an empty auditorium

items.example: Zara feels lonely when nobody is backstage with her.
items.note: Say 'lonely' when you feel sad because you are by yourself.

image.describe: a small calico cat sitting quietly by itself on a wooden bench in a quiet dressing room

items.example: Tom felt embarrassed when he dropped the box on stage.
items.note: Use 'embarrassed' when your face turns red after a silly mistake.

image.describe: a striped cat with pink cheeks covering its eyes with one paw next to a spilled box of props

practice.prompt: Mia is about to sing in front of a big audience for the first time. How does she feel?
practice.explanation: Before performing in front of many people, it is natural to feel nervous.

practice.prompt: Listen and choose the sentence you hear.
practice.audio: Leo is proud of his new costume.
practice.answer: Leo is proud of his new costume.
options: Leo is proud of his new costume.
Leo is angry about his new costume.
Leo is nervous in his new costume.
practice.explanation: Leo feels great about his costume, so he is proud.

practice.prompt: Match each situation with the best emotion.

pairs.left: You have no friends with you
You made a big mistake on stage

practice.explanation: Match the feeling to the situation: lonely without friends, embarrassed after a mistake, jealous of a prize, and angry about a broken pen.

practice.prompt: Sam wants the big part that Leo got. Complete the sentence.
practice.explanation: Use 'jealous' when someone wants what another person has.

practice.prompt: Put the words in order to tell why Ben is upset.
practice.answer: Ben is angry because he lost his key.
practice.explanation: Subject + is + angry + because + reason.

practice.prompt: Tom walked onto the stage in the wrong hat and everyone looked at him. Complete the sentence.
practice.explanation: A silly mistake in front of others makes you feel embarrassed.

practice.prompt: Everyone went home after rehearsal, and Zara stayed backstage. Complete the sentence.
practice.explanation: Being all by yourself can make you feel lonely.

practice.prompt: Say this sentence out loud.
practice.text: I am proud of our team.
practice.answer: I am proud of our team.
practice.explanation: Use 'proud of' to show you feel happy about someone's good work.

story.hook: Why is everyone backstage feeling so many different emotions today?

image.describe: Backstage at a cozy theatre: Smarty the black cat talks with Mia, Leo, Sam, Ben, Zara, and Tom among costumes and stage props.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Hello, everyone! How do you feel before our first rehearsal?

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: I am nervous, Smarty! The stage looks so big.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: I am thrilled and very proud of my costume.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: I feel a bit jealous because Leo has the best hat.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: And I am angry and upset! I lost my notebook.

lines.speaker: Tom
lines.text: Here it is, Ben! Sorry, I dropped it earlier. I felt so embarrassed.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Oh, I am relieved! Thanks, Tom. Do not feel disappointed, Zara—come rehearse with us so you are not lonely!

questions.prompt: Why is Mia nervous?
questions.explanation: Mia says she is nervous because the stage looks big.

questions.prompt: How does Sam feel about Leo's hat?
questions.explanation: Sam says he feels a bit jealous because Leo has the best hat.

questions.prompt: Why was Tom embarrassed?
questions.explanation: Tom dropped Ben's notebook earlier and felt embarrassed.

mission.setup: Smarty asks how you feel before going on stage at the theatre.

turns.smarty: Welcome backstage! How do you feel before a big show?
turns.hint: Say 'I feel nervous' or 'I am proud'.

turns.smarty: Tom dropped his hat on stage! How does he feel now?
turns.hint: Say 'He feels embarrassed' or 'He is embarrassed'.

turns.smarty: You did a great job on stage! Are you proud?

exposure.gloss: very excited and happy
unhappy or worried
sad because something was not as good as hoped

lessons.title: Moods
lessons.scenario: A rainy afternoon rehearsal at the theatre puts everyone in a different mood.

items.example: Lily is in a good mood because the sun came out.
items.note: Say 'in a good mood' when someone feels cheerful and happy.

items.example: Let us buy some cake to cheer up Omar.
items.note: Use 'cheer up' when you try to make yourself or a friend feel happier.

items.example: Please calm down and drink some water.
items.note: Say 'calm down' to help someone stop feeling angry or nervous.

items.example: Omar is fed up with waiting in the rain.
items.note: Use 'fed up' when you are tired and annoyed because something has gone on too long.

items.example: Sam says he does not like soup, and I could not care less.
items.note: Say 'I could not care less' when something is not important to you at all.

items.example: Mia is on edge before her big song.
items.note: Use 'on edge' when you feel tense and cannot relax.

practice.prompt: Lily is singing and helping everyone backstage. How is she feeling?
practice.explanation: Someone who is happy and cheerful is in a good mood.

practice.prompt: Listen and choose what Smarty says.
practice.audio: Take a seat and calm down.
practice.answer: Take a seat and calm down.
options: Take a seat and calm down.
Take a seat and cheer up.
practice.explanation: 'Calm down' means to relax when you are nervous or angry.

practice.prompt: Match each phrase with its meaning.
practice.explanation: Cheer up means feel happier, calm down means relax, fed up means annoyed, and on edge means nervous.

practice.prompt: We have rehearsed the same scene ten times! Complete the sentence.
practice.text: I am ___ with practising this scene.
practice.explanation: Use 'fed up' when you are tired and annoyed by repeating something.

practice.prompt: Build a sentence that shows you do not care about the rain.
practice.answer: I could not care less about the rain.
practice.explanation: 'I could not care less' means it does not bother you at all.

practice.prompt: Mia cannot sit still before the show starts. Complete the sentence.
practice.explanation: When someone is tense and nervous, they are on edge.

practice.prompt: Omar looks unhappy. Tell him to feel happier.
practice.explanation: Say 'Cheer up' to help a friend feel happier.

practice.prompt: Say this sentence out loud.
practice.text: I am in a good mood.
practice.answer: I am in a good mood.
practice.explanation: Say 'I am in a good mood' when you feel happy.

story.hook: Can Smarty help his friends feel better on a rainy rehearsal afternoon?

image.describe: Inside a warm theatre lounge with rain on the window: Smarty the black cat offers tea to Omar, Mia, Lily, and Sam.

lines.speaker: Lily
lines.text: Good afternoon, Smarty! I am in a good mood today.

lines.speaker: Omar
lines.text: Well, I am grumpy and fed up with this rain!

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Cheer up, Omar! Have some hot chocolate.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: I am so restless and on edge about my song.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Calm down, Mia. You practised all week, and you are carefree when you sing!

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The rain? I could not care less! Let us rehearse!

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Thanks, Smarty. Now I feel ready, and Omar is not tearful any more!

questions.prompt: Why is Omar fed up?
questions.explanation: Omar says he is fed up with the rain.

questions.prompt: What does Smarty tell Mia to do?
questions.explanation: Mia is on edge about her song, so Smarty tells her to calm down.

questions.prompt: How does Sam feel about the rain?
options: He is fed up with it.
He is on edge about it.
questions.explanation: Sam says 'I could not care less!' about the rain.

mission.setup: Smarty checks on your mood before rehearsal.

turns.smarty: How is your mood right now?
turns.example: I am in a good mood.
turns.hint: Say 'I am in a good mood', 'I am fed up', or 'I am on edge'.

turns.smarty: Omar is unhappy because it is raining. What do you say to him?
turns.hint: Tell Omar to cheer up.

turns.smarty: Mia is nervous and speaking too fast. What do you tell her?
turns.hint: Tell Mia to calm down.

exposure.gloss: in a bad mood and easily annoyed
almost crying
having no worries
unable to stay still or relax

lessons.title: He must be
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Ana find clues backstage at the theatre and guess who left them.

items.example: Leo is smiling, so he must be in a good mood.
items.note: Use 'must be' when you are almost sure something is true right now.

items.example: Mia is quiet, so she might be nervous.
items.note: Say 'might be' when something is possible, but you are not sure.

items.example: It can not be Leo's hat because his hat is blue.
items.note: Use 'can not be' when you are almost sure something is impossible.

items.example: The lights are on, so they may be on stage.
items.note: Say 'may be' to make a polite, possible guess about now.

items.example: Whose scarf is this? It could be Zara's.
items.note: Use 'could be' when there is a chance something is true.

items.example: Snow in July? You must be joking!
items.note: Say 'You must be joking' when someone says something surprising or hard to believe.

grammar.title: Guessing about now: must, might, may, could, can not
grammar.explanation: Use 'must be' when clues make you 95% sure. Use 'might be', 'may be', or 'could be' when something is possible (about 50% sure). Use 'can not be' when you are 95% sure it is impossible.
examples: He has been working all day, so he must be tired.
She is not here yet; she might be on the bus.
It can not be midnight—the sun is still out!

practice.prompt: Ben ran all the way to the theatre and has no water. How sure are you that he is thirsty?
practice.explanation: Running without water is a strong clue, so use 'He must be'.

practice.prompt: Listen and choose the sentence you hear.
practice.audio: It can not be Ben because he is at home.
practice.answer: It can not be Ben because he is at home.
options: It can not be Ben because he is at home.
It must be Ben because he is at home.
It could be Ben because he is at home.
practice.explanation: If Ben is at home, it is impossible for him to be here, so use 'It can not be'.

practice.prompt: Match each phrase with how sure you are.
practice.explanation: Must be = sure yes, might be = possible, can not be = sure no, you must be joking = disbelief.

practice.prompt: Zara is not in the room. Maybe she is in the café. Complete the sentence.
practice.explanation: When something is possible, use 'She might be'.

practice.prompt: Leo and Sam are not backstage. Maybe they are on stage. Complete the sentence.
practice.explanation: For two people when something is possible, use 'They may be'.

practice.prompt: Build a guess about the red scarf on the table.
practice.explanation: 'It could be' shows a possible guess.

practice.prompt: Sam says he ate ten pizzas for lunch! What do you say?
practice.explanation: Say 'You must be joking!' when someone says something hard to believe.

practice.prompt: Say this guess out loud.
practice.text: He must be in a good mood.
practice.answer: He must be in a good mood.
practice.explanation: Use 'He must be' when you are sure from the clues.

story.hook: Whose red scarf is on the chair backstage, and where is everyone?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat and Ana examine a red scarf on a backstage chair while hearing violin music through a door.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Look at this red scarf, Smarty. Whose is it?

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: It can not be Ben's—he never wears red. It could be Mia's!

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Listen! Someone is playing the violin behind that door.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: The evidence is obvious! That is Omar's favourite song, so he must be in there.

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Where are Mia and Lily? Presumably they are still at the café.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Yes, they may be having tea. Or she might be on stage already!

lines.speaker: Ana
lines.text: Mia on stage an hour early? That is unlikely—you must be joking!

questions.prompt: Why does Smarty say the scarf can not be Ben's?
options: Because Ben is at the café.
questions.explanation: Smarty says 'It can not be Ben's—he never wears red.'

questions.prompt: Who does Smarty think is playing the violin?
questions.explanation: It is Omar's favourite song, so Smarty says 'he must be in there.'

questions.prompt: What does Ana say when Smarty guesses Mia is on stage early?
questions.explanation: Ana does not believe Mia is on stage an hour early, so she says 'You must be joking!'

mission.setup: Smarty shows you clues backstage and asks for your guesses.

turns.smarty: Leo just won a prize and is smiling! How does he feel?
turns.hint: Say 'He must be proud' or 'He must be happy'.

turns.smarty: Mia is not backstage. Where is she?
accept: ^she must be (?:on stage|at the cafe|at home)$
turns.hint: Say 'She might be on stage' or 'She may be at the café'.

turns.smarty: Look! A pink hat! Is it Tom's hat?
turns.example: It can not be his hat.
turns.hint: Say 'It can not be his hat.'

exposure.gloss: easy to see or understand
facts or clues that show something is true
probably, based on what you know
not probable

lessons.title: Review
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Mia review emotions, moods, and guesses while watching rehearsal.

practice.prompt: Tom tripped on stage and his face turned red. How did he feel?
practice.explanation: Making a mistake in front of others makes you feel embarrassed.

practice.prompt: Listen and choose the sentence you hear.
practice.audio: Cheer up and calm down before the show.
practice.answer: Cheer up and calm down before the show.
options: Cheer up and calm down before the show.
Fed up and on edge before the show.
In a good mood before the show.
practice.explanation: Cheer up means feel happier, and calm down means relax.

practice.prompt: Match the clues with Smarty's guesses.

pairs.right: He must be in a good mood

pairs.left: That coat is way too small for Sam
pairs.right: It can not be Sam's coat

pairs.left: Whose notebook is on the chair?

practice.explanation: Match the level of certainty to each clue.

practice.prompt: Ben has waited for the bus for an hour. Complete the sentence.
practice.explanation: 'Fed up' means annoyed because something has taken too long.

practice.prompt: Build a sentence guessing how Mia feels.
practice.answer: She might be on edge now.
practice.explanation: She + might be + on edge.

practice.prompt: Zara has nobody to sit with at lunch. Complete the sentence.
practice.explanation: Sitting without friends makes someone feel lonely.

practice.prompt: Say this phrase out loud.
practice.explanation: Use this phrase when something sounds impossible or funny.

story.hook: Why is Ben standing alone by the stage door?

image.describe: Smarty the black cat and Mia watch Ben standing by the theatre stage door with a worried look.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Look at Ben by the door, Smarty. He is not in a good mood.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: He might be nervous about his lines, or he could be lonely.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: He looks a bit angry too. He must be fed up with waiting.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Let us go speak to him! We can help him cheer up and calm down.

lines.speaker: Ben
lines.text: Oh, hi! I was on edge because I thought rehearsal was cancelled!

questions.explanation: Ben says he was on edge because he thought rehearsal was cancelled.

questions.explanation: Mia says everyone is on stage right now.

turns.smarty: Zara is by herself and looks sad. How does she feel?

turns.smarty: How can we help a friend who is angry?
turns.hint: Use 'calm down'.

turns.smarty: Leo is smiling after rehearsal. Make a guess about his mood!
turns.example: He must be in a good mood.
turns.hint: Say 'He must be in a good mood' or 'He must be proud'.

lessons.title: Family life
lessons.scenario: During a break at the theatre, Sam and Zara chat with Smarty about their families.

items.example: I get on with my brother very well.
items.note: Say 'get on with' when you have a friendly relationship with someone.

items.example: Zara looks up to her older sister because she is kind and clever.
items.note: Use 'look up to' when you admire and like someone.

items.example: My grandparents helped bring up my cousins.
items.note: Say 'bring up' when parents or family care for children until they are adults.

items.example: Sam and his sister grew up in a small town.
items.note: Use 'grow up' to talk about changing from a child into an adult.

items.example: Leo takes after his father—both love music.
items.note: Say 'take after' when you look or act like an older family member.

items.example: I never fall out with my best friend for long.
items.note: Use 'fall out with' when you argue with someone and stop being friendly for a while.

practice.prompt: Mia has curly hair and a great sense of humour, just like her mother. Which phrase fits?
practice.explanation: 'Take after' means to look or behave like a parent or older relative.

practice.prompt: Listen and choose what you hear.
practice.audio: I really look up to my grandmother.
practice.answer: I really look up to my grandmother.
options: I really look up to my grandmother.
I really take after my grandmother.
I really get on with my grandmother.
practice.explanation: 'Look up to' means to admire and like someone.

practice.prompt: Match each phrasal verb with its meaning.

pairs.right: care for a child as they grow

practice.explanation: Get on with = be friendly, look up to = admire, bring up = raise a child, fall out with = argue.

practice.prompt: Where did your parents spend their childhood? Complete the question.
practice.explanation: 'Grow up' means to spend your childhood and become an adult.

practice.prompt: Build a sentence about Sam and his cousin.
practice.answer: Sam gets on with his cousin.
practice.explanation: Sam + gets on with + his cousin.

practice.prompt: Parents work hard to care for their children. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: It takes love and patience to ___ a child.
practice.explanation: Parents 'bring up' their children.

practice.prompt: Ben was angry with Tom yesterday, so they stopped speaking. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: Ben did not want to ___ Tom.
practice.explanation: 'Fall out with' means to argue and stop being friendly.

practice.prompt: Say this sentence out loud.
practice.explanation: Say 'I take after my mother' when you are like her.

story.hook: Who in Zara's family inspired her to act on stage?

image.describe: Backstage on a cozy sofa, Smarty the black cat listens as Zara and Sam look at a family photo.

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: You act so well, Zara! Do you take after someone in your family?

lines.speaker: Zara
lines.text: Yes! My aunt is an actress, and I really look up to her.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That is great! Did you grow up in the same household?

lines.speaker: Zara

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Do you get on with every relative in your family?

lines.speaker: Zara
lines.text: Yes! Sometimes I fall out with my younger sibling about music, but we are proud of each other.

questions.prompt: Who does Zara look up to?
questions.explanation: Zara says her aunt is an actress and she looks up to her.

questions.prompt: Where did Zara's parents bring her up?
questions.explanation: Zara says 'my parents brought me up near the sea.'

questions.prompt: Why does Zara sometimes fall out with her younger sibling?
questions.explanation: Zara says she sometimes falls out with her younger sibling about music.

mission.setup: Smarty asks you about your family and friends.

turns.smarty: Do you get on with your family?

turns.example: Yes, I get on with my family.
turns.hint: Say 'Yes, I get on with my family.'

a person in your family

lessons.title: Love
lessons.scenario: Smarty explains the relationship story in the theatre play to Leo and Mia.

items.example: In the play, the hero and the singer fall in love.
items.note: Say 'fall in love' when two people start having deep romantic feelings for each other.

items.example: They decided to get engaged in spring.
items.note: Use 'get engaged' when two people agree to get married each other.

items.example: They are going to get married at a big wedding in June.
items.note: Say 'get married' when two people become husband and wife at a wedding.

items.example: Why did that couple split up last year?
items.note: Use 'split up' when two people end their relationship.

items.example: Ana and Omar make a very happy couple.
items.note: Say 'a couple' for two people who are in a relationship together.

items.example: Tom started to go out with his best friend's cousin.
items.note: Use 'go out with' when you spend time together as boyfriend and girlfriend.

practice.prompt: Two people are together in a relationship. What do we call them?
practice.explanation: Two people in a relationship are called 'a couple'.

practice.prompt: Listen and choose the sentence you hear.
practice.audio: They got engaged after two years together.
practice.answer: They got engaged after two years together.
options: They got engaged after two years together.
They split up after two years together.
They fell in love after two years together.
practice.explanation: 'Got engaged' means they agreed to get married.

practice.prompt: Match each relationship phrase with what happens.
practice.explanation: Go out with = date, fall in love = start loving, get engaged = agree to marry, split up = stop going out together.

practice.prompt: The wedding is this Saturday! Complete the sentence.
practice.text: They are going to ___ on Saturday.
practice.explanation: People get married at a wedding.

practice.prompt: Build a sentence about the characters in the story.
practice.answer: They fall in love at the station.
practice.explanation: They + fall in love + at the station.

practice.prompt: The two characters argued and ended their relationship. Complete the sentence.
practice.explanation: 'Split up' means to stop going out together.

practice.prompt: Before getting engaged, people usually date each other. Complete the sentence.
practice.explanation: 'Go out with' means to date someone.

practice.prompt: Say this sentence out loud.
practice.explanation: Say 'a happy couple' for two people who are happy together.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Smarty, tell us what happens to the romantic couple in our play!

lines.text: First, the hero meets his partner at a café, and he asks to go out with her.

lines.speaker: Leo
lines.text: Do they fall in love right away?

lines.speaker: Smarty
lines.text: Yes! Soon he is her fiance and she is his fiancee because they get engaged.

lines.speaker: Mia
lines.text: Oh no, do they split up in the second part?

lines.speaker: Smarty

questions.prompt: Where does the hero first meet his partner?

questions.prompt: What happens after they fall in love?

turns.smarty: In our play, two people meet and like each other. What happens next?
turns.hint: Say 'They fall in love' or 'They become a couple'.

turns.smarty: They want to have a wedding next summer! What do they do first?
turns.hint: Say 'They get engaged.'

turns.smarty: And what happens at the happy ending of the play?
turns.hint: Say 'They get married.'

exposure.gloss: the woman someone is engaged to marry
the man someone is engaged to marry
showing love and affection
the person you are in a relationship with

lessons.title: Advice
lessons.scenario: Ben fell out with Tom before rehearsal and asks Smarty and Mia for advice.

items.example: You should try speaking to Tom after rehearsal.
items.note: Say 'You should try...' to give helpful, friendly advice.

items.example: Why do not you send him a nice message?
items.note: Use 'Why do not you...' to suggest an easy idea.

items.example: It might help to say sorry first.
items.note: Say 'It might help to...' when you want to give gentle advice.

items.example: I have a problem with my lines—what do you suggest?
items.note: Ask 'What do you suggest?' when you want someone's advice.

items.text: If I were in your shoes
items.example: If I were in your shoes, I would call him.
items.note: Say 'If I were in your shoes' to tell what you would do in their place.

items.example: Have you thought about writing him a note?
items.note: Ask 'Have you thought about...' to offer a new idea gently.

grammar.title: Patterns for giving advice
grammar.explanation: Notice what comes after each phrase: 'Why do not you' and 'It might help to' take the base verb (go, call, say). 'Have you thought about' takes a noun or -ing verb (writing, speaking). 'You should try' can take -ing or to + verb.
examples: Why do not you call him?
It might help to take a rest.
Have you thought about practising together?

practice.prompt: You have a problem and want Smarty's advice. What do you ask?
practice.explanation: Ask 'What do you suggest?' when you want ideas or advice.

practice.prompt: Listen and choose the sentence you hear.
practice.audio: If I were in your shoes, I would say sorry.
practice.answer: If I were in your shoes, I would say sorry.
options: If I were in your shoes, I would say sorry.
If I had your shoes, I would go home.
Why do not you wear your new shoes?
practice.explanation: 'If I were in your shoes' means 'If I were in your situation'.

practice.prompt: Match the beginnings and endings of these advice sentences.
practice.explanation: Check the verb form after each phrase: base verb after 'Why do not you' and 'It might help to', and -ing after 'Have you thought about'.

practice.prompt: Mia is nervous about her song. Give her friendly advice.
practice.explanation: 'You should try' goes well with 'practising' (-ing).

practice.prompt: Suggest asking Smarty for help. Complete the question.
options: If I were in your shoes
practice.explanation: 'Why do not you' is followed by the base verb 'ask'.

practice.prompt: Build a sentence giving gentle advice.
practice.answer: It might help to drink some tea.
practice.explanation: It might help to + base verb (drink).

practice.prompt: Offer a new idea to a friend who fell out with his brother.
practice.explanation: 'Have you thought about' is followed by the -ing form 'speaking'.

lessons.title: Verb patterns
lessons.scenario: Smarty gives final reminders to the cast before opening night at the theatre.

items.example: Please remember to bring your costume tomorrow.
items.note: Use 'remember to' when you do not forget to do something important.

items.example: Do not forget to speak loudly on stage.
items.note: Say 'forget to' when someone does not remember to do something.

items.example: You should stop doing homework so late at night.
items.note: Use 'stop' + -ing when you quit an activity.

items.example: If you feel nervous, try reading a funny book.
items.note: Say 'try' + -ing when you test a new idea to see if it helps.

items.example: I am used to working late before a big show.
items.note: Say 'I am used to' + -ing when something feels normal because you have done it often.

items.example: We look forward to meeting the audience after the play.
items.note: Use 'look forward to' + -ing or a noun when you feel excited about something in the future.

grammar.title: Verbs followed by 'to' or '-ing'
grammar.explanation: Use 'to + verb' for things you need to do ('remember to bring', 'forget to call'). Use '-ing' after 'stop', 'try' (for an experiment), 'be used to', and 'look forward to' ('stop working', 'look forward to meeting').
examples: Stop working so hard and take a rest.
I look forward to seeing you!
